title: How I'm using AI to build art, cutscenes and a tutorial for my fantasy TCG (Steam playtest now open)
author: EsconAmatin
selftext:
The playtest is auto-approved if you want to try the tutorial: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4804280/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4804280/)



I'm making "Astralight: Pilgrim's Duel", a fantasy deckbuilding TCG, and I just shipped a tutorial and opened a Steam playtest. AI is used across almost every resource in the game, so I wanted to share what the workflow actually looks like and what kept breaking.



Characters and battlers

Most character art starts as an AI draft. I run Qwen image editing locally through ComfyUI for everyday edits, and only fall back to GPT image generation when the local model keeps failing. The biggest recurring problem was style drift: every regeneration made heads a little bigger and bodies a little shorter until characters stopped looking like themselves. What fixed it was always editing from the original image instead of stacking edits on top of generated results, and comparing every new version side by side with the reference. Noise also builds up fast when you re-edit outputs, so every prompt explicitly asks for clean flat coloring with no grainy texture. Cutouts and outlines go through Photoshop, because my Python heuristics for background removal never held up.



Cutscenes and the story trailer

The trailer and the tutorial opening are made from AI stills turned into short clips with a first/last-frame video model. The model loved adding zoom-ins, sparkles and drifting dust that I never asked for. For calm shots like a campfire at night, I gave up on generating the whole clip: I kept the still image fixed and only animated the fire, and did the dawn light change procedurally. Subtitles are in 13 languages.



The tutorial

The new tutorial puts the Drill Instructor on screen as a visual-novel character in the middle of the first battle. He pauses the game and walks you through mulligan, life, mana, attacking, End Turn and AUTO, hiding himself for a moment while a box highlights each part of the UI. Getting dialogue to render above the battle UI took a render-texture trick, and the scenes themselves were missing from builds until I hooked the dialogue engine's resource registration into the build pipeline.



I'm curious how others handle character consistency over dozens of regenerations, and whether anyone has found a video model that respects "no camera movement".
